content: Avalanche transceivers are specialized radio devices designed to locate individuals or equipment buried under snow. These devices are commonly referred to as ARVAs (Appareil de Recherche de Victimes en Avalanche in French), avalanche beacons, or avalanche transceivers, with various regional slang terms also in use. When in transmission mode, the device emits a pulsed radio signal that can be detected by another transceiver. The nature of the radio pulse allows the user of the receiving transceiver to orient the device and pinpoint the location of the transmitting beacon using techniques akin to radio direction finding. The current international standard for these devices specifies a frequency of 457 kHz, and numerous manufacturers produce beacons that adhere to this standard. It is critical to understand that an avalanche beacon is not a preventative tool for avoiding burial in an avalanche but rather a means to minimize the time a person remains buried. In 1968, Dr. John Lawton developed the first effective avalanche transceiver at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York. The initial units were sold in 1971 under the brand name Skadi. These early devices operated at a frequency of 275 kHz and converted the radio signal into an audible tone that could be heard by the user. By following the tone to its loudest point, the operator could locate the buried beacon using a grid search technique. In 1986, the International Commission for Alpine Rescue (IKAR) adopted the 457 kHz frequency as the standard, which was later formalized by ASTM in 1996. The standard includes specifications such as 200 hours of transmission at +10°C, one hour of reception at -10°C, operational temperature ranges from -20°C to +45°C, a pulse period of 1000 ms ± 300 ms, and a frequency tolerance of ±80 Hz. There are two main types of avalanche beacons: analog and digital. Both types comply with the international standard but differ in how they convey the location of the buried beacon to the user. Analog Beacons: The original avalanche beacons were analog devices that transmitted the pulsed signal as an audible tone. The tone's volume increased as the user approached the transmitting beacon. Some analog beacons were later enhanced with visual indicators, such as LEDs, to display signal strength, and earpieces to improve the user's ability to hear the tone. Digital Beacons: Digital beacons analyze the strength of the received signal and the emitted dipole flux pattern to calculate both the distance and direction to the buried transceiver. This information is then displayed to the user, making the search process more intuitive. Search Techniques: The highly directional nature of the 457 kHz signal at the ranges typical for avalanche burial has led to the development of various search techniques. Proficiency in beacon use is considered a professional responsibility for recreational backcountry skiers, mountaineers, and avalanche professionals such as ski guides, ski patrollers, and search-and-rescue personnel. Both recreational users and professionals regularly participate in drills, practice sessions, and scenarios as part of avalanche skills training. For a single burial scenario, search methods may include: Grid search Induction search Circle method These techniques can be adapted and extended to situations involving multiple burials.
